design_detail: Narrative review by a single author (Annual Review of Clinical Psychology) arguing that remission from drug dependence is common, usually happens without treatment, and occurs with a constant yearly probability. Its core numbers are the author's own secondary calculations: remission recomputed as (lifetime − 12-month prevalence)/lifetime prevalence from published figures of four US national surveys (ECA 1980–84, NCS 1990–92, NCS-R 2001–03, NESARC 2001–02); an exponential model fitted to NESARC cumulative remission curves for cocaine, cannabis (marijuana), alcohol and nicotine dependence (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011, and yearly probabilities supplied by that group); and eight treatment follow-up series found by a key-word search. Heroin enters only through Winick (1962) and the Vietnam study (Robins, 1993). No systematic search for the review as a whole; correlates of remission are reviewed selectively, by the author's own account (p. 48).
can_establish: That in four US national household surveys most people who had ever met DSM criteria for drug dependence did not meet them in the past year (76% to 83% in the three later surveys; 57% for abuse or dependence in the ECA), and that in NESARC the recalled time from onset of dependence to remission was much shorter for cocaine and cannabis (half by about 4 and 6 years) than for alcohol and nicotine (16 and about 30 years).
cannot_establish: That people stopped using drugs (remission meant not meeting dependence criteria, or in the ECA having no symptoms, for a year, one drug at a time); that remission lasts (the surveys are single interviews); that treatment adds nothing (treatment and remission were not related in these data, as the author says, p. 42); or anything specific to heroin or other opioids, which are not among the NESARC drugs analysed.

sample.recruitment: Four US national surveys of psychiatric disorders with samples meant to approximate the US population: ECA (five metropolitan sites, nearly 20,000 people interviewed 1980–84, including people in prisons and other institutions), NCS (about 8,100, early 1990s), NCS-R (about 9,200, 2001–03) and NESARC (about 43,000, 2001–02) (pp. 34–36). Treatment follow-up series: eight series from studies with three or more post-treatment evaluations and at least 70% retention (p. 43). Vietnam veterans: Robins (1993) and later follow-ups of the same men (pp. 42, 44–45).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Surveys: the four national surveys conducted after the revised DSM criteria (p. 34). Treatment studies: key-word search ('longitudinal', 'remission', 'follow-up', 'addiction or drug dependence'), kept if three or more post-treatment evaluations and at least 70% of participants retained; databases, dates, languages and screening not reported (p. 43).
sample.attrition: Survey response rates are not reported in the review. Treatment series: missing participants handled by taking the midpoint between the remission rate among people re-interviewed and the rate in the original sample (pp. 43–44).
sample.selection_effects: The surveys after the ECA did not sample people in jails and prisons; Compton et al. (2010), as summarized, estimate drug-dependence prevalence about 25% higher with them included (p. 46). People who keep using heavily may be less likely to take part, harder to find or more likely to have died (pp. 43, 45). The treatment series are a non-systematic selection of high-retention studies. Correlates of remission are reviewed selectively (p. 48).

exposure.measurement: Lay-interviewer structured DSM interviews (for example, a screening question on using heroin on one's own more than five times, followed by symptom questions; p. 34); NESARC also asked when each symptom first appeared and when it stopped (p. 38). DSM-IV dependence: three or more of seven listed symptoms within 12 months (p. 33). Criteria editions differed across surveys (p. 37).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported; remission is defined by symptom counts, not by amounts used.
exposure.polysubstance: Remission is counted drug by drug: a person in remission from cocaine dependence could be dependent on another drug and could relapse later (p. 39). The ECA combined abuse and dependence on any drug into one category (p. 35).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not measured. 'Remission' meant no symptoms in the past year (ECA) or two or fewer dependence symptoms in the past year (NCS, NCS-R, NESARC) (p. 37); it does not mean abstinence.

comparison.controls: Within-survey comparisons by drug, sex, age group and race/ethnicity; remission from the other ECA psychiatric disorders as a check that high drug remission was not produced by the survey method (Figure 1b, p. 36).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable; respondents' characteristics before onset are not analysed beyond demographic correlates (Arndt et al., 2010, as summarized, p. 48).

outcomes.instruments: Lifetime and 12-month prevalence of DSM drug abuse and dependence from published survey summaries; NESARC cumulative probability of remission and yearly (conditional) probability of remitting by years since onset of dependence (Figures 3–5); remission or abstinence in treatment follow-ups (Figure 6); current cases by age (Figure 7).
outcomes.validity_norms: The author cites interclinician reliability of DSM criteria and an ECA test–retest study of 325 respondents a year apart, in which lay-interviewer and psychiatrist diagnoses predicted wave-2 outcomes equally well (pp. 33, 47). Self-report against biological tests is discussed narratively (pp. 46–47).
outcomes.operationalization: Remission: once met criteria but not in the past 12 months, computed as (lifetime % − 12-month %)/lifetime %; a remitted person could relapse the next year (p. 34). In the NESARC curves, people who had remitted but met criteria again at interview were not counted as remitted (p. 39). Treatment: mentioning drug use to a health specialist (ECA) or a broad list from 12-step groups and social services to methadone and religious counselling (NESARC) (pp. 41–42).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable (no hypothesis tests are reported).

analysis.effect_sizes: No confidence intervals anywhere. Share of lifetime cases not current: ECA 57% (abuse and/or dependence), NCS 76%, NCS-R 83%, NESARC 81% (dependence) (pp. 35, 37). NESARC model fits, cumulative remission = A(1 − e^(−r × years since onset)): cocaine A 0.98, r 0.17; cannabis 0.94, 0.13; alcohol 0.95, 0.05; cigarettes 1.38, 0.015, or with A fixed at 1.00, r 0.024 (R² 0.98) (Figure 3, p. 38; p. 39). Half remitted by year 4 (cocaine), 6 (cannabis), 16 (alcohol) and about 30 (cigarettes); two-thirds by year 7 (cocaine), 27 (alcohol) and 49 (cigarettes) (p. 39). Cumulative remission 10 and 15 years after onset: nicotine 20% and 28%, alcohol 40% and 49%, cannabis 69% and 81%, cocaine 79% and 89% (p. 42). Expected duration of dependence, 1/r: about 6, 8, 20 and 42 years (p. 53). Cocaine by race/ethnicity: white A 0.98, r 0.21; Hispanic 0.96, 0.17; Black 1.04, 0.09 (Figure 5, p. 41).
analysis.covariates: None in the author's own analyses. For race, he cites Arndt et al. (2010), in whose multivariable models race/ethnicity no longer predicted remission once marital status and high-school completion were included (p. 48).
analysis.selective_reporting: Model fit is described only as an error term below 1% (cocaine; cigarettes) and R² 0.98 (cigarettes, asymptote fixed) (p. 39); the observed values behind Figures 3–5 are not tabulated; the yearly probabilities in Figure 4 are unpublished data supplied by the NESARC authors (p. 40). Heroin and other opioids are not among the drugs analysed.
analysis.power: Not applicable. The author notes that yearly probabilities for cocaine and cannabis scatter more at long durations because few people remain dependent (p. 40).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In US household surveys most people who had ever met DSM criteria for drug dependence did not meet them in the past year. In NESARC, recalled time to remission was short for cocaine and cannabis dependence (half by about 4 and 6 years after onset) and long for alcohol and nicotine dependence (16 and about 30 years), with a minority dependent for decades (5% for at least 23 years for cocaine, 36 for cannabis). A constant-yearly-probability curve describes the cumulative curves closely. Few people with current dependence were in treatment (no more than 16% in NESARC; at most 30% of ECA cases had mentioned drug use to a health specialist).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The summary points say addiction is not a chronic relapsing disease (Summary Point 1; also p. 37), and the abstract and summary points that most people addicted to illicit drugs were no longer using them at clinically significant levels by about age 30, and that remission does not require treatment (pp. 29, 53). Several steps go beyond the data. (1) The title's 'quitting' and 'no longer using at clinically significant levels' rest on not meeting dependence criteria in the past year, drug by drug, which allows continued use and dependence on another drug (pp. 34, 39). (2) The survey curves cover cocaine, cannabis, alcohol and nicotine; heroin enters only through Winick (1962) and the Vietnam veterans, whom the author treats as plausibly a random sample of healthy American men aged 18 to 25 (p. 42), although Robins (1993, p. 1051) stresses that few of them would have become addicted had they stayed in the US. (3) 'Does not require treatment' is inferred from low treatment rates, while the author concedes that treatment and remission had not been related in population data (p. 42); the Vietnam contrast of treated and untreated men does not allow for who sought treatment. (4) The constant-probability claim rests on fitted curves without uncertainty; Figure 4 shows the fitted cannabis line falling from about 0.13 to about 0.03 over 40 years (read from the figure), a slope near zero only in absolute terms. (5) The calculation for missed people (p. 46) concerns the overall remission rate but is used to defend 'quit by about age 30'. (6) Stability of remission is inferred partly from rising cumulative curves (p. 43), which, being cumulative, cannot fall, and from Figure 7, whose values appear to be an age distribution of current cases (see reporting issues). The abstract's statement that about 5% went on using cocaine heavily well into their forties (p. 29) is, in the body, 5% dependent for at least 23 years (p. 48).

timeline.event: Winick's analysis of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics register for 1955–59: by age 37, 73% of people once listed for heroin addiction had gone from the register; Heyman says Winick wrongly assumed the register was complete and that those who left had stopped (Heyman, p. 31).

Vaillant's 20-year follow-up of 100 men treated for narcotic addiction at the Lexington US Public Health Service Hospital: years addicted did not appear to change the odds of becoming abstinent over the next five years (as quoted by Heyman, p. 52).
Robins's lecture on the Vietnam veterans: of men addicted in Vietnam, 5% were addicted in the first year after return and 12% at any time in 3 years; few were treated (robins_1993, p. 1045).
Compton et al. letter: omitting people in jails and prisons means drug-dependence prevalence is about 25% higher than household surveys report (as summarized by Heyman, p. 46).

Lopez-Quintero et al., NESARC study of the probability and predictors of remission from lifetime nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence (Addiction 106:657–69), the source of Figures 3 and 5; no project record (the project's lopez-quintero_2011 is a different 2011 paper by the same group, on transition from first use to dependence).
Moos and Finney commentary questioning survey remission rates (single interviews; people who stop are likelier to take part), summarized and answered by Heyman (p. 43).
Vergés et al.: the likelihood of remitting from alcohol dependence changed little with time since onset (as summarized by Heyman, p. 52).
Systematic review and meta-analysis of remission from substance use disorders (Fleury et al., 2016; project record, not read for this card).

replication.where_it_stands: A high share of lifetime drug-dependence cases not current at interview is consistent across the three later US surveys (76% to 83%). What it means for individuals is less settled: remission here is cross-sectional and drug by drug, does not mean abstinence, and the people the surveys miss (in prison, homeless, dead) may be those who remit least. By the author's own account, whether treatment adds to remission in community samples had not been tested by 2013 (p. 42). The constant-yearly-probability model is presented without uncertainty estimates, and heroin and other opioids are not covered by the NESARC curves; the primary NESARC remission paper (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011) is not among the project's files.

funding.declared_conflicts: The author is not aware of any affiliations, memberships, funding or financial holdings that might be perceived as affecting the objectivity of the review (Disclosure statement, p. 55).
funding.affiliations_note: Gene M. Heyman, Department of Psychology, Boston College (p. 29). The review cites the author's 2009 book (Addiction: A Disorder of Choice) and closes with a decision-making interpretation of remission (pp. 51–53). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the review.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective population cohort, including people who use opioids, that diagnoses drug use disorders repeatedly over decades, follows people into prison and hard-to-reach settings, records amounts used and treatment received, and estimates remission, relapse and their dependence on time since onset with confidence intervals; with the effect of treatment on remission estimated with adjustment for severity and demographic factors.

domains.note: No systematic search for the review. The four surveys are a defensible frame (the national surveys using revised DSM criteria), but the treatment series come from a key-word search without databases, dates or screening (p. 43), and correlates of remission are reviewed selectively by the author's own account (p. 48).

Limits of the survey data (self-report, missed populations, temporary remission) are discussed and partly quantified (pp. 43–47); no formal appraisal; the treatment series are heterogeneous and combined with an ad hoc midpoint rule for missing participants (pp. 43–44).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The core numbers are the author's own recalculations and model fits from other researchers' published or supplied data, not independent studies; the choice-based interpretation draws on his 2009 book.

Explanations (availability, legal status, choice) are mostly offered as interpretations, and the author says the smoking trend graph cannot show a causal link (p. 51); but the summary points state that remission does not require treatment as a logical inference (p. 53), although the treatment–remission relation was untested (p. 42).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on whether addiction is chronic
domains.note: Treatment follow-ups showing long courses are acknowledged and placed at one end of a single distribution, and a critique of survey remission (Moos & Finney, 2011) is summarized and answered; evidence that treatment helps is represented only by uncontrolled follow-ups.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used, and the overall judgment follows the worst domain. The review is explicit about many limits of survey data and quantifies some, but its selection is unsystematic, its central numbers are the author's recalculations without uncertainty, and its strongest conclusions (a constant probability of remission; remission without treatment) rest on inference. Cite it for the survey remission figures with their definitions (preferably with the primary surveys), not for 'quitting' drugs or for treatment being unnecessary.

key_findings.finding: Remission was calculated by the author from published survey figures as (lifetime % − 12-month %)/lifetime %, i.e. the share of people who once met dependence criteria but had not in the past year; a person counted as remitted could relapse the following year.
key_findings.locator: Background and Definitions › How to Define Remission (one paragraph)

key_findings.finding: ECA (1980–84; nearly 20,000 people interviewed): 57% of people who had ever met criteria for drug abuse and/or dependence had no symptoms in the past year, women more often than men; about 50% at ages 18–29 and more than 80% at 64 or older. For the non-drug psychiatric disorders in the ECA, the remitted share never exceeded 50% in any age group.
key_findings.locator: Remission from Drug Dependence › The ECA Findings, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 35, continuing on p. 36); Figure 1 (p. 36)
key_findings.note: The text says the age trend could reflect stable remission or cohort differences, since the ECA was not longitudinal (p. 36). See reporting issues on Figure 1.

key_findings.finding: Among people who had ever met criteria for drug dependence, 76% (NCS 1990–92, about 8,100 people), 83% (NCS-R 2001–03, about 9,200) and 81% (NESARC 2001–02, about 43,000) did not meet them in the past year. The author attributes the lower ECA figure to its stricter rule (no symptoms, against two or fewer dependence symptoms in the later surveys) and to its combining abuse with dependence.
key_findings.locator: Are the ECA Remission Rates Reliable?, 1st, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Figure 2 (p. 37)

key_findings.finding: NESARC, counted from the recalled onset of dependence: half of people ever dependent on cocaine had remitted by year 4 and half of those dependent on cannabis by year 6, against year 16 for alcohol and about 30 years for cigarettes; two-thirds had remitted by year 7 for cocaine, year 27 for alcohol and year 49 for cigarettes.
key_findings.locator: Remission as a Function of Onset of Dependence, Drug Type, and Ethnicity, 2nd paragraph (begins on p. 38)
key_findings.note: The cannabis half-way point is given as year 7 on p. 48 and as 55% by six years on p. 53.

key_findings.finding: A constant-yearly-probability (exponential) model was fitted to the cumulative remission curves: cocaine 0.98(1 − e^(−0.17 × years)), cannabis 0.94(1 − e^(−0.13 × years)), alcohol 0.95(1 − e^(−0.05 × years)), cigarettes 1.38(1 − e^(−0.015 × years)), and for cigarettes with the asymptote fixed at 1.00, r 0.024 (R² 0.98). The error term was under 1% for cocaine and for cigarettes; the author calls the free cigarette asymptote of 1.38 not sensible, since the maximum is 1.0, and notes that observed quitting rose above the fixed-asymptote curve at about 55 years.
key_findings.locator: Figure 3 (p. 38); Remission as a Function of Onset of Dependence, Drug Type, and Ethnicity, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 39)
key_findings.note: The text describes the cocaine fit as 99% eventual remission with exponent 0.16 (p. 39), against 0.98 and 0.17 printed in Figure 3.

key_findings.finding: Ten years after onset (on average about age 30), cumulative remission was 20% for nicotine, 40% for alcohol, 69% for cannabis and 79% for cocaine dependence; at 15 years (about age 35), 28%, 49%, 81% and 89%.
key_findings.locator: Remission from Drug Dependence › Age 30 (one paragraph)

key_findings.finding: Summary point: of people addicted to cocaine, 27% had remitted after two years, 51% after four and 76% after nine; for cannabis, 55% by six years and 75% by twelve. With onset typically at about 20, the author concludes that most were no longer using drugs at clinically significant levels by age 30.

A minority stayed dependent much longer: of people dependent on cocaine, 10% for at least 16 years and 5% for at least 23; of people dependent on cannabis, 10% for at least 23 years and 5% for at least 36. The abstract restates the cocaine figure as about 5% still using cocaine heavily well into their forties.
key_findings.locator: Differences in Remission Rates, 1st paragraph; Abstract (p. 29)

key_findings.finding: Yearly (conditional) probabilities of remitting, from unpublished NESARC data supplied by the authors, had fitted slopes close to zero (average absolute deviation from zero 0.0008; steepest, cannabis, −0.002), which the author reads as a probability of remitting independent of time since onset; cocaine and cannabis values scatter more at long durations, which he attributes to shrinking numbers.
key_findings.locator: The Probability of Remitting, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Figure 4
key_findings.note: Read from Figure 4 (approximate): the fitted cannabis line falls from about 0.13 at onset to about 0.03 at 40 years, the cocaine line from about 0.15 to about 0.12; cigarette values lie at about 0.02 to 0.03.

key_findings.finding: From the constant probability the author argues that theories giving a large role to drug-induced neural adaptations predict falling remission with continued use, and that the stationary probabilities were independent of cumulative drug exposure; he also says no theory predicted this shape and that it has no ready explanation.
key_findings.locator: Differences in Remission Rates, 1st paragraph (p. 48); Summary Points, 5 (p. 53); Future Issues, 1 (p. 54)

key_findings.finding: Cocaine dependence by race/ethnicity (NESARC): fitted curves 0.98(1 − e^(−0.21 × years)) for white, 0.96(1 − e^(−0.17 × years)) for Hispanic and 1.04(1 − e^(−0.09 × years)) for Black respondents; about 50% of white respondents had remitted by year 3, Black respondents not until year 8. In Arndt et al. (2010), as summarized, race/ethnicity no longer predicted remission once marital status and high-school completion were in the model.
key_findings.locator: Figure 5 and Racial/Ethnic Differences in Remission Rates (p. 41); Differences in Remission Rates › Racial/Ethnic Differences in Remission (p. 48)

key_findings.finding: Treatment was uncommon: in the ECA, 30% of people who met criteria for drug abuse or dependence had mentioned their drug use to a health specialist, which the author treats as an upper bound for treatment; in NESARC, with treatment broadly defined (12-step groups, social services, inpatient care, detoxification, methadone, emergency care, religious counselling), no more than 16% of people currently meeting criteria were in treatment. The author states that the relation between treatment and remission in population samples had not been published.
key_findings.locator: Remission from Drug Dependence › Treatment, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Citing Robins (1993): of men meeting criteria for opiate dependence at departure from Vietnam, 6% reported treatment and their one-year relapse rate was nearly 70%, against under 12% for the 94% not treated; remission among men dependent in Vietnam was 95%, 88% and 96% at 1, 3 and 24 years, with reports confirmed by urine and/or hair tests (Robins, 1993; Ledgerwood et al., 2008; Price et al., 2009).
key_findings.locator: Treatment, 3rd paragraph (p. 42); Remission Stability in Treatment Follow-Up Studies, 3rd paragraph (p. 44, continuing on p. 45)
key_findings.note: Robins (1993, p. 1045) gives 6% as the share of men urine-positive at departure who entered drug treatment after return, and 12% as the share of all men addicted in Vietnam re-addicted at any time in 3 years; see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: If the surveys missed 25% of people with dependence (Compton et al., 2010) and none of them remitted, overall remission in NCS-R and NESARC would fall from about 80% to about 64%; if half of them remitted by about age 37, it would be about 74%. For the true rate to be 20%, there would have to be three uncounted people for every one counted, none remitted: about one in ten US adults ever addicted to an illicit drug and almost 20 million more current cases (lifetime prevalence of substance dependence taken as about 2.8%; adult population 238 million).
key_findings.locator: Methodological Issues › Calculating the Impact of Missing Addicts, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: In the 1996 follow-up of the Vietnam veterans, 6% reported opiate use in the past 90 days while hair tests showed 4.5% (Ledgerwood et al., 2008, as summarized), which the author offers as an example of self-reports exceeding biological tests.
key_findings.locator: On the Validity of Self-Report in Epidemiological Surveys, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Eight treatment follow-up series (three or more evaluations, at least 70% retention; missing participants handled by the midpoint rule) mostly showed remission or abstinence rising across evaluations, from about 14% to 63% at the first evaluation to about 38% to 79% at the last (read from Figure 6); the author takes the rise as evidence that remission is stable. Studies differed widely, from all-male samples with more than 90% prison records (Vaillant) to a sample 77% female with many from high-status backgrounds (Zanarini et al., 2011).
key_findings.locator: Are the Remission Rates Stable?, 2nd paragraph (p. 43); Remission Stability in Treatment Follow-Up Studies, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 6 (p. 44)
key_findings.note: Two series dip at their last evaluation (Dias et al., 2008, about 52% to 50%; Teesson et al., 2008, about 70% to 67%; read from Figure 6).

key_findings.finding: Remission was much lower for legal than for illegal drugs; the author argues that availability, including legal status, is the simplest explanation, citing history: after the 1914 Harrison Act, laudanum drinkers and opium smokers all but disappeared, the laudanum drinkers seeking treatment or somehow stopping rather than switching to heroin (less is known about the opium smokers), and in Canada a Prohibition-era rise in alcohol prices was followed by a deep dip in consumption and about a one-third drop in cirrhosis cases (Seeley, 1960, as summarized). [p. 49 says both groups all but disappeared; 'from the record' is not in the text.]
key_findings.locator: Drug Differences in Remission, 2nd paragraph (p. 49); Legislation, Opiate Addiction, and Remission, 2nd paragraph (p. 49); Legislation, Alcoholism, and Remission (Prohibition), 2nd paragraph (p. 50)

reporting_issues.issue: The text says the Figure 4 intercept for cigarettes is about 0.11 and that this is the Figure 3 constant (p. 40), but Figure 3 prints 0.015 (free asymptote) and 0.024 (asymptote fixed at 1.0), Summary point 3 gives an expected duration of about 42 years (1/r, so r about 0.024; p. 53), and the cigarette points and fitted line in Figure 4 lie at about 0.02 to 0.03 (read from the figure).
reporting_issues.consequence: The 0.11 is an error: a yearly probability of 0.11 would imply a half-life of about 6 years (editors' calculation, ln 2/0.11), not the 30 years reported on p. 39. The cigarette constant is about 0.02.

reporting_issues.issue: The cocaine fit is described in the text as 99% eventual remission with exponent 0.16 (p. 39), and 0.16 is called the Figure 3 constant (p. 40), but Figure 3 prints 0.98 and 0.17; the cocaine line in Figure 4 starts at about 0.15, not the 0.17 stated (read from the figure).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the values differ in the second decimal place. Cite Figure 3's printed values.

reporting_issues.issue: The time by which half of people dependent on cannabis had remitted is given as 6 years (p. 39), as year 7 (p. 48) and as 55% by six years (p. 53).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; 'about 6 to 7 years' is what the review supports.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 1: in panel b, the ECA remission share at ages 18–29 is about 52%, below both the male (about 57%) and female (about 71%) values for the same age group in panel a (read from the figure); a combined figure cannot lie below both sex-specific ones if the panels describe the same cases. The text's 'about 50%' follows panel b.
reporting_issues.consequence: The youngest-group ECA remission is uncertain (somewhere between about 50% and 70%); the overall 57% is unaffected.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 7 ('current' cases by age): the values read from the figure sum to about 100% within each survey (ECA about 70, 28 and 2; NCS about 48, 23, 19 and 10; NESARC about 48, 34, 16 and 3), which suggests the y-axis gives the share of all current cases falling in each age group, not the share of each age group's lifetime cases still current; the text reads the steep decline as evidence that remission is stable (p. 45). Read the other way, the ECA youngest-group value (about 70% current) would also contradict about 50% remitted in Figure 1. The legend dates NESARC 2000–2001, against 2001–02 elsewhere (pp. 34, 37).
reporting_issues.consequence: If the figure is an age distribution of current cases, the decline with age also reflects how many people in each age group ever became dependent (cohort differences), and the figure cannot by itself show that remission is stable.

reporting_issues.issue: The Vietnam figures are restated inaccurately (p. 42). Robins (1993) gives 6% as the share of men urine-positive at departure who entered drug treatment after return, not of men meeting opiate-dependence criteria (p. 1045); reports that two-thirds of those treated had relapsed by the time of interview (p. 1046); and gives 12% as the share of all men addicted in Vietnam who were re-addicted at any time in the 3 years after return, not as the relapse rate of the untreated 94% (p. 1045).
reporting_issues.consequence: The treated-versus-untreated contrast (nearly 70% against under 12%) mixes denominators and time frames. Robins herself reads treated cases as people who cannot stop on their own (Robins, 1993, p. 1050), so the contrast cannot show that treatment fails or is unnecessary.

reporting_issues.issue: Fitted asymptotes above 1 (an eventual remission share above 100%): cigarettes 1.38, which the author discusses, and Black respondents with cocaine dependence 1.04 (Figure 5), which he does not.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the asymptotes are unconstrained, so A cannot always be read as the share who will eventually remit.

reporting_issues.issue: Model fit is described only as an error term below 1% (not defined) and one R² (0.98); no confidence intervals are given for A or r, no test of the zero slopes in Figure 4 is reported, and the observed values are not tabulated (pp. 39–40). Read relative to the cannabis rate constant (0.13, Figure 3), a slope of −0.002 per year would lower the yearly probability by about 0.08 over 40 years, roughly 60% (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: The claim that the probability of remitting is constant cannot be checked for precision, and for cannabis it holds only in absolute terms.

reporting_issues.issue: The 'typical' duration of six to eight years before quitting (p. 52) is not derived in the text; it matches the expected durations 1/r for cocaine and cannabis (about 6 and 8 years, p. 53), which are means of the fitted curves, whereas the medians are about 4 and 6 years (p. 39).
reporting_issues.consequence: Readers may take six to eight years as the typical (median) duration; half of people remitted sooner.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record, Annual Review of Clinical Psychology 9:29–59, a downloaded copy with the volume's contents pages appended), pp. 29–59 (all pages; text and Figures 1–8 checked on rendered pages, Figures 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7 enlarged at 300 dpi; values marked as read from a figure are approximate; no supplement). Paragraphs are counted within the smallest printed heading.
